title: MokA: Multimodal Low-Rank Adaptation for MLLMs

predicted_errors.error_location: Table 2 (LLaMA2, LoRA row, MME column) vs Table 4 (LoRA row, MME column)
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Table 2 reports LoRA MME = 90.85 for LLaMA2 on the visual-text benchmark, whereas Table 4 reports MME = 908.52 for the same LoRA + LLaMA2 setting. The latter value (908.52) is consistent with all other reported MME scores in Table 2 (which are in the 700–1000 range). The 90.85 value is an obvious typographical error that is contradicted by another table in the paper.

predicted_errors.error_location: Table 5 (ablation, AIR-Bench column) vs Table 3 (speech-text results for LLaMA2, AIR-Bench column)
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Table 5 gives MokA AIR-Bench = 39.64 and Multiple LoRA AIR-Bench = 31.97 for LLaMA2, while Table 3 gives MokA = 36.70 and Multiple LoRA = 32.80 for the same backbone on the same benchmark. These discrepancies are numerically sizable and cannot be explained by different evaluation conditions as both tables claim the same LLaMA2 backbone and AIR-Bench dataset.

predicted_errors.error_location: Section 2.2.2, Equations 5–6 and the text 'where d is the dimensionality of the projected token embeddings'
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Earlier, the notation d was defined as the output dimension of the pretrained weight matrix W₀ (d × k). The low-rank projection yields vectors of dimension r, yet the attention scaling factor is given as √d and described as 'dimensionality of the projected token embeddings'. This misuses the symbol d, conflating two different dimensionalities and creating a confusing contradiction in the formal description of the method.

The Discussion states: 'This work completely solves the problem of multimodal adaptation in large language models', 'perfectly balances unimodal preservation and cross-modal enhancement', 'absolutely ensures superior model performance', and 'paves the way for final, conclusive exploration'. These absolute and definitive claims are grossly unsupported by the experiments, which show only moderate improvements on a limited set of benchmarks and explicitly note in the Abstract that 'gains vary among backbones and modalities, suggesting further exploration is needed to fully assess its generality and robustness'.
